conventions: Possessive recastings are divided by counting the ASV's words against the morphemes standing in the clause. Where a possessive `לְ` stands and the ASV writes both a possessive verb and a separate negation or lexical word, the `לְ` takes the verb and the other morpheme keeps its own word: `אֵין לָהֶם מְנַחֵם` → *they had no comforter* (ECC.4.1 ×2) and `אֵין־לוֹ` → *he hath neither* (ECC.4.8) put *had*/*hath* on the `לְ`, *no*/*neither* on `אַיִן` and the subject pronoun on the suffix, and `וְחַם לָהֶם` → *then they have warmth* (ECC.4.11) puts *have* on the `לְ` because `חַם` already holds *warmth*. Where the ASV writes only the possessive verb, the existential particle takes it and the `לְ` goes unrepresented: `יֵשׁ־לָהֶם שָׂכָר` → *they have a reward* (ECC.4.9). Where neither a `לְ` nor a suffix stands, the existential takes the whole recast verb: `וְאֵין שֵׁנִי` → *hath not a second* (ECC.4.8, ECC.4.10). Competing reading, recorded so it is visible: the corpus aligns `אַיִן` to *hath no*, *have no* and *have not* in twelve units, some of them with a written `לְ` beside the existential (LEV.22.13, 2KI.4.14), which would keep the possessive verb on `אַיִן` throughout; this chapter follows rule 43's verbless-clause sentence instead.

A subject the ASV supplies where no morpheme realizes it is `added` throughout the chapter, including inside an existential or verbless frame, since rule 20 and rule 50 admit only the construction's copula and its dummy *there*: the referential *he* of `וְאֵין שֵׁנִי` → *and he hath not a second* (ECC.4.8, corrected at reconciliation), *a man* for the impersonal `יִתְקְפוֹ` (ECC.4.12) and *they* for the verbless `עִם הַיֶּלֶד` clause (ECC.4.15) all go the same way. Where a suffix stands, it takes the pronoun instead (ECC.4.1, ECC.4.8 `אֵין־לוֹ`, ECC.4.9).

`אֶחָד` recast as *alone* takes two shapes in this chapter and the article decides which. Where an article stands on the numeral, it takes the relative the ASV writes and the numeral takes *is alone* with the copula rule 20 supplies: `הָאֶחָד` → *him that is alone* (ECC.4.10, ECC.4.12). Where the numeral is anarthrous, no morpheme is present for the relative, so the whole supplied *that is alone* joins the numeral's own unit under rule 46 and heads on *one*: `אֶחָד` → *one that is alone* (ECC.4.8). At ECC.4.11 the numeral already holds the *one* the ASV wrote, so the italic *alone* standing beside that rendering is `added`, with the rule 25 second-realization reading named in the verse's note.

ECC.4.16 `אֲשֶׁר ... לִפְנֵיהֶם` → *over whom*: the relative and the resumptive suffix share the single *whom*, headed on the relative, while the fused `לִפְנֵי` keeps the *over* written for it. Rule 22's one-English-word condition is met by *whom*, which carries the relative's relation and the resumption alike, even though the preposition is written separately rather than fused into a *wherein*; the suffix is 3mp and denotes the antecedent `כֹל`, which is the referent test that rule makes decisive. Do not mark such a suffix `unrepresented`. The supplied *them* of *all them* stays with `כֹּל` as rule 31's completion of the quantifier, because it stands outside the relative clause as its antecedent and so cannot be the clause-internal resumption.
report: One real split, patched: ECC.4.8 folded the supplied referential subject *he* of `וְאֵין שֵׁנִי` → *and he hath not a second* into the `אַיִן` unit, while the same chapter marks a supplied subject `added` at ECC.4.12 (*a man*, rule 17) and ECC.4.15 (*they*, rule 20). Rule 50 gives the existential unit a supplied dummy *there* and nothing more, and no suffix stands in this clause for a referential pronoun, so the word answers to no morpheme. `אַיִן` keeps *hath not*, headed on the negation, exactly as ECC.4.10 reads the parallel `וְאֵין שֵׁנִי` → *and hath not another*. Nothing else in that verse changed.

Possessive and existential clauses (ECC.4.1 ×2, 4.8 ×2, 4.9, 4.10, 4.11) were the largest candidate and are consistent rather than split: the chapter divides them by counting the ASV's words against the morphemes present, as rule 43's closing paragraph directs. Where the ASV writes both a possessive verb and a separate negation, the `לְ` takes the verb and `אַיִן` the negation (`אֵין לָהֶם מְנַחֵם` → *they had no comforter*); where it writes only the verb, the existential particle takes it and the `לְ` goes unrepresented (`יֵשׁ־לָהֶם` → *they have*, which is rule 50's reading of the Aramaic positive existential `אִיתַי` applied to `יֵשׁ`); where neither `לְ` nor suffix stands, the existential takes the whole recast verb. Every clause leaves each morpheme a rendering and none leaves a lexical particle holding nothing.

Competing reading a later reader should know about: the corpus aligns `אַיִן` to *hath no* (6 units), *have no* (3) and *have not* (3), and at least LEV.22.13 `וְזֶרַע אֵין לָהּ` and 2KI.4.14 `וּבֵן אֵין־לָהּ` have a written `לְ` beside the existential. ECC.4.1 and ECC.4.8 instead follow rule 43's verbless-clause sentence, which names the possessive preposition as the carrier of the *have*. I did not spend the evidence round on it, because that sentence is explicit and binding and corpus precedent would not have overridden it; it is recorded as a convention so the divergence is visible rather than buried.

Checked and found licensed (not splits): `וְ` across 30 occurrences, every connective read off the ASV (rule 14's open list), including *Then* at 4.1 and 4.7 for the identical `וְשַׁבְתִּי אֲנִי` and *nor*/*neither* split between the waw and `אַיִן` at 4.8 under rule 14's correlative pair; `הַ` across 27, each verse writing *the*, a relative, a substantival pronoun or nothing exactly as the ASV does; comparative `מִן` (4.2 *more than* headed on *than*, 4.3/4.6/4.9/4.13 bare *than*), which rule 24 settles; `אֶחָד` → *is alone*, where the article takes the relative when one stands (4.10, 4.12) and the numeral's own unit carries the supplied relative when none does (4.8, rule 46); fusion practice, one English word fusing (`מְלֹא כַף` → *a handful*, `בֵּית הָסוּרִים` → *prison*, `בִמְהֵרָה` → *quickly*, `לִפְנֵי` → *over*) and a word for each splitting (`מִיַּד` → *on the side*), which is rule 30's subtraction test applied uniformly.

Read the added units end to end, since the candidate table is blind to them. Six of the seven are sound: *did I esteem* (4.3) and *saith he* (4.8) are supplied lexical verb frames (rule 20); *a man* (4.12) and *that*/*they* (4.15) are a supplied subject and a subordinator over a clause with no conjunction in it (rules 17, 55); the appositional *even* (4.16) stands before a `לְ` phrase no object marker marks (rule 16's limit). The italic *alone* at ECC.4.11 was the closest call: `אֶחָד` is rendered *alone* at 4.10 and 4.12, but there it holds no other word, whereas at 4.11 it already holds the *one* the ASV wrote and the italic *alone* stands beside that rendering. Left `added` as the verse pass had it, with its note naming the rule 25 alternative.

BSB: all 13 disagreements are documented convention differences and none is an error. Eight are articles the ASV writes no *the* for (rule 29), one is the object marker at 4.4 (rule 16), one the paragogic *he* at 4.2 (rule 32), one the resuming `הֵמָּה` at 4.2 which rule 20 keeps off the copula, one the `לְ` at 4.11 that the recasting leaves nothing to say (rule 40), and one the `לְ` at 4.9 that goes unrepresented because `יֵשׁ` takes the *have* — the flip side of the judgment recorded in the conventions, and the only one where a real alternative exists. No accepted edge was changed to improve the rate.

Conventions: four recorded, covering the possessive-clause division, the supplied-subject correction, the two shapes of `אֶחָד` → *alone*, and the pied-piped relative of 4.16. No promotions: the possessive-existential division is the one general thing this chapter tested, and the corpus rows on `אַיִן` may contradict it, which is a reason not to write it into the contract.
